issues.legal_issue: A comprehensive suit for specific performance and consequential relief is not barred merely because a statutory procedure is available to obtain registration of an executed instrument.
material_facts: The purchaser sued for specific performance of an executed but unregistered sale deed and also sought injunction or, alternatively, possession.
The vendor refused to cooperate with registration, and the deed had not been presented to the registering officer.
The suit sought relief beyond registration alone.
issues.conclusion: The suit was maintainable, and the statutory registration procedure did not bar the claim for specific performance and consequential relief.
issues.legal_principle: The court held that the registration procedure under Sections 23–26, 32, 72, 73, 76 and 77 of the Registration Act, 1908, provides a remedy for obtaining registration in the circumstances specified by those provisions. Where the statutory stages have been reached and the only relief sought is registration, that procedure may be exclusive. A suit for specific performance is broader, however, and may include consequential relief; the registration procedure does not supersede that remedy. The court considered divergent High Court authorities, including Manicka Gounder v. Elumalai Gounder, Ramachandra Naidu v. Ramaiah Naidu, Veeran Ambalam v. Vellaiammal, Ellammal v. Rangaswamy Koundar, Mathai v. Joseph and Veerappa Naidu v. Venkaiah.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A claimant brings a suit to enforce an agreement to transfer immovable property.
predicates.seeks_consequential_relief: The claimant seeks relief beyond obtaining registration of the instrument, such as possession or an injunction.
predicates.registration_procedure_not_reached: The instrument has not been presented for registration, so the statutory steps for seeking registration have not yet occurred.

issues.definition: When a suit seeks specific performance and either includes consequential relief or is brought before the registration procedure has been reached, the suit is not barred by that procedure.

issues.legal_issue: An unregistered instrument recording a transfer agreement may be received in evidence to prove the agreement, although it does not itself effect the transfer.
material_facts: The purchaser relied on an executed but unregistered sale deed as evidence of the parties’ agreement to transfer the property.
The first appellate court found that witnesses reliably proved execution of the deed and payment of the stated consideration.
The purchaser sought specific performance rather than relying on the unregistered deed as a completed registered transfer.
issues.conclusion: The unregistered deed could be received in evidence to prove the agreement between the parties, and that agreement could support a claim for specific performance.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 49 of the Registration Act, 1908, the unregistered deed could be received in evidence to prove the agreement between the parties, though it did not itself constitute a transfer of the property. An agreement to transfer immovable property may be specifically enforced under the Specific Relief Act. The court upheld the first appellate court’s reliance on the deed in that evidentiary capacity.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A claimant brings a suit to enforce an agreement to transfer immovable property.
predicates.unregistered_transfer_instrument: The parties executed an instrument recording a transfer of immovable property, but it was not registered.
predicates.instrument_relied_on_to_prove_agreement: The claimant relies on the instrument as evidence of the parties’ agreement rather than as a completed transfer of the property.

issues.definition: In a specific-performance suit, an unregistered transfer instrument relied on as evidence of the parties’ agreement is admissible to prove that agreement, but not as proof that the property was transferred.
